newsitem.title: USA: Clinton wields new power to cancel budget items.
newsitem.headline: Clinton wields new power to cancel budget items.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Monday wielded a new presidential power to strike three provisions from the balanced-budget accord, saying he wanted to end the Washington game of catering to special interests.

Clinton's action was the first exercise of the line-item veto, a power sought by U.S. presidents for more than a century to cancel parts of spending bills and to strike down narrowly-targeted tax breaks.

The three provisions -- two special-interest tax breaks and an item affecting Medicaid spending in New York state -- will save the federal government some $600 million over five years, a pittance beside its $1.7 trillion annual budget.

The move drew the ire of Republican Speaker of the House House of Representatives Newt Gingrich, historically an ardent supporter of the line-item veto, who accused the president of having negotiated the balanced-budget deal in bad faith.

The president took aim at two tax provisions: one that would have allowed financial services companies to shelter income in foreign tax havens and a second that would have given a tax break to certain food processing businesses.

He also struck down a provision that would have reduced the state of New York's spending on the Medicaid health care programme for the poor, prompting protests from Sen. Alfonse D'Amato and Gov. George Pataki, both New York Republicans.

"The actions that I take today will save the American people hundreds of millions of dollars ... and send a signal that the Washington rules have changed for good," Clinton said as he signed the vetoes at the White House. "From now on presidents will be able to say 'no' to wasteful spending or tax loopholes even as they say 'yes' to vital legislation."
The veto has long been championed by the Republicans, who included it in their "Contract with America" manifesto before they won control of both houses of Congress in 1994.

Congress passed the line-item veto last year, giving the power to Clinton, a Democrat, but stipulating he could not use it until Jan. 1, 1997. Congress can ultimately overturn a veto with two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate.
Gingrich's office issued a statement in the name of his spokeswoman Christina Martin expressing dismay at the vetoes.
"Disappointment and surprise are the usual side effects of having been blind-sided and today's line-item veto announcement is no exception," Martin said.

She said Gingrich and other Republicans had once believed the White House bargained in good faith before reaching the budget accord signed into law last week that aims to balance the federal budget by 2002 while cutting taxes by $95 billion.

"Now it appears that may not have been the case. No objections to these provisions were raised throughout the talks, therefore these vetoes may have less to do with sound policy and more to do with petty politics," she said.
White House officials denied the vetoes were political and said they informed Gingrich of their decision to use the veto.
They also offered the following details on the financial effect of the vetoes on the budget over the next five years:
-- cancelling the provision to allow U.S. financial services firms to avoid paying taxes on income from overseas operations would save the federal government $317 million;
-- vetoing the tax break to food processing companies that sell assets to certain farmers' cooperatives will save the government an estimated $98 milliion over five years;
-- and striking down preferential treatment for the state of New York regarding the Medicaid health care programme for the poor would save the federal government some $200 million.
Sen. D'Amato of New York, sometimes known as "Senator Pothole" for his aggressive defence of the interests of his constituents, reacted immediately.

"We're surprised and disappointed that the president would veto a provision that provides health care for the poorest New Yorkers and we will look at every possible means to reverse this decision," D'Amato said in a statement.
The White House officials said legal challenges may be filed against the line-item veto but that they were confident it would be found to be Constitutional.

The Supreme Court in June dismissed a challenge to the line-item veto filed by six members of Congress. The court did not rule on the merits of such a veto but said the members who filed the case lacked the legal standing to bring the suit.
